catalog_quote: Heath 2003, sec. 2.1 (p. 335): "Makaa has eleven vowels, twenty-two consonants, and two phonemic tone levels (table 18.1)." Sec. 2.4 Tones (p. 337): "Mikaá is a tonal language, with contrastive high and low, e.g. Ø-kà 'wicker' (C5) and L-ká 'leaf' (C7). The tones may occur singly or in sequences, resulting in high-low and low–high tone sequences, e.g. kâ 'down there' and ... 'eating'. A high tone may be lowered in certain environments, which results in downstep, e.g. ... 'I have seen', or in downdrift. Some morphemes have polar tone, e.g. àlâm 'beloved one' where the tone of the nominalizing prefix a- is opposite to the following tone. Some syllables are analysed as being toneless, e.g. ki 'to go'; if they do not receive a grammatical tone, they receive a default low tone." new_statements.rule_in_words: Both first-hand phonological descriptions (Heath & Heath 1982; Heath 2003) analyse Makaa word prosody exclusively as lexical/grammatical tone (H vs L, contours, floating tones, downstep); neither states a word-stress or accent position, nor explicitly denies stress. The only positional asymmetry noted is distributional: long vowels and labialized/palatalized onsets are confined to the first syllable of the radical (1982: 10-11, 42-43), i.e. the usual NW-Bantu stem-initial prominence, but the authors do not call it stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tone: toneless syllables get default L; polar-tone prefixes; complex L-HL pattern only word-finally.)
new_statements.domain_note: No stress domain discussed. Tone patterns are stated over the radical in isolation (1982) and the word/verbal complex (2003). Description is of the Mbwaanz dialect (1982 explicitly; 2003 by the same authors).
new_statements.identity_note: Both Heath sources describe the Mbwaanz dialect of Makaa (A83, maka1304), spoken along the Abong-Mbang-Mayos road; Heath 2003 lists four dialects (Mbwaanz, Bibend, Shikunda, Besip) forming a chain with Bikele/Kol (A832) to the south and Byep/North Makaa (A831, byep1241, ISO mkk) to the north - neither of those is covered here. Afane Otsaga 1999 'meka.. du Gabon' may not be this language. Vermeir 2024's accent statement is for Sso (A82), not Makaa.

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2 Phonology (pp. 335-337) covers segments, vowel length, syllable types, morphophonemics and sec. 2.4 'Tones' ('Makaa is a tonal language, with contrastive high and low.. downstep.. downdrift.. polar tone.. toneless syllables'); a full-text search for stress/accent the whole chapter for stress/accent/prominence/penult/intonation = 0 hits. Word prosody treated exclusively as tone.
